cards.explanation: The answer is to hold a feast to Him in the wilderness. Moses, Israel's leader, and Aaron walk up to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, with a message. They say the LORD, the God of Israel, says, “Let My people go, so that they may hold a feast to Me in the wilderness.” (Exodus 5:1) A feast, for the LORD. Now THAT is an invitation, and Pharaoh gets handed the best one ever and doesn't even RSVP.

The answer is that Pharaoh asks who the LORD is that he should obey Him. Pharaoh, king of Egypt, says, “Who is the LORD that I should obey His voice and let Israel go?” (Exodus 5:2) He doesn't ask about travel plans or schedules. He goes straight at who the LORD is, and he says he doesn't know Him.

The answer is True. Moses, Israel's leader, and Aaron ask Pharaoh, king of Egypt, to let them go on a three-day journey to sacrifice to the LORD, “…or He may strike us with plagues or with the sword.” (Exodus 5:3) They say it right to the king's face. That takes nerve, friends, and I'd have been hiding behind my own mustache.

The answer is that Moses and Aaron would stop a lot of workers. Pharaoh, king of Egypt, says, “Look, the people of the land are now numerous, and you would be stopping them from their labor.” (Exodus 5:5) His point is about the work getting held up. A big crew means a big pause.

The answer is straw. Pharaoh, king of Egypt, says, “You shall no longer supply the people with straw for making bricks.” (Exodus 5:7) Straw is one small ingredient, and he takes that away without lowering anything else. Little things matter when you're making a whole pile of bricks.

The answer is False. Pharaoh, king of Egypt, tells the taskmasters, “But require of them the same quota of bricks as before; do not reduce it.” (Exodus 5:8) The people lose the straw supply, but the number of bricks stays the same. Less help, same load.

The answer is lazy. Pharaoh, king of Egypt, says, “For they are lazy; that is why they are crying out, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to our God.’” (Exodus 5:8) That's what Pharaoh calls them. Notice he's the one saying it, and he's the one handing out the orders.

The answer is True. Pharaoh, king of Egypt, says, “Make the work harder on the men so they will be occupied and pay no attention to these lies.” (Exodus 5:9) He calls it lies, and he wants the men occupied. I think he's hoping heavy work leaves no room for listening. Nothing about that order is gentle.

The answer is all over the land of Egypt. “So the people scattered all over the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw.” (Exodus 5:12) Scattered is a good word for it. Picture a whole workforce heading off in every direction after the same thing. Me, I can't even find the right spatula in my own bakery.

The answer is True, friends, and this part is heavy. The Israelite foremen, whom Pharaoh's taskmasters had set over the people, were beaten and asked, “Why have you not fulfilled your quota of bricks yesterday or today, as you did before?” (Exodus 5:14) The foremen are the ones beaten and questioned. I think this one hurts.

The answer is people. The Israelite foremen say, “Look, your servants are being beaten, but the fault is with your own people.” (Exodus 5:16) They're speaking to Pharaoh, the king of Egypt. They say it right to his face, and I think that took nerve.

The answer is False. Pharaoh, king of Egypt, tells the foremen, “Now get to work. You will be given no straw, yet you must deliver the full quota of bricks.” (Exodus 5:18) There's no bargain here. He repeats the order and sends them back.

The answer is that the foremen ask the LORD to look on Moses and Aaron and judge them. The foremen say, “May the LORD look upon you and judge you…” (Exodus 5:21) They say it to Moses and Aaron, who were standing there waiting for them. That's a tough greeting after the day they've had.

The answer is True, and it's a heavy one. The foremen say to Moses and Aaron, “you have placed in their hand a sword to kill us!” (Exodus 5:21) The word “their” points to Pharaoh and his officials. I think the foremen are scared, and the words sound like it.

The answer is, “Why have You brought trouble upon this people?” Moses, Israel's leader, asks, “Lord, why have You brought trouble upon this people?” (Exodus 5:22) He takes the question straight to the LORD instead of keeping it to himself. When something doesn't make sense, that's a good place to bring it.

The answer is True. Right after asking why, Moses, Israel's leader, adds, “Is this why You sent me?” (Exodus 5:22) That's an honest question, and he says it to the LORD Himself. I think he's trying to make sense of a hard day.

The answer is delivered. Moses, Israel's leader, says, “…and You have not delivered Your people in any way.” (Exodus 5:23) He says it in the LORD's presence. That's Moses being honest about how things look to him.

The answer is what the LORD will do to Pharaoh. The LORD says to Moses, “Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh…” (Exodus 6:1) Moses brought a hard question, and the LORD answers by pointing to what He will do. The answer is the LORD's own action.

The answer is that Pharaoh will drive them out of his land. The LORD says, “because of My strong hand he will drive them out of his land.” (Exodus 6:1) Pharaoh, king of Egypt, was saying no a few verses ago, and now the LORD says he will drive them out. That is a big turn.
